analysis.one_liner: Forces pharmacy benefits managers to pay pharmacies the full cost of drugs, ban spread pricing and steering, and pass rebates to patients.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 55 cosponsors to rein in pharmacy benefits managers died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a floor on what pharmacy benefits managers (PBMs) — the middlemen who process prescription drug claims for insurers and employers — must pay pharmacies for drugs covered by Medicare Part D, Medicare Advantage drug plans, Medicaid managed care, federal employee health plans, and TRICARE. It would ban PBMs from 'spread pricing' (charging the program more than they pay the pharmacy), from steering patients to PBMs' own affiliated pharmacies, and from charging pharmacies fees after a claim is filed. It would also require at least 80% of manufacturer rebates to reduce what patients pay at the counter, and would make knowing violations a federal felony with civil whistleblower suits allowed. The bill was referred to four House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in Medicare Part D, Medicare Advantage drug plans, Medicaid managed care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, and TRICARE, who would pay less out of pocket at the pharmacy counter and could not be pushed to a PBM-owned pharmacy. Community and independent pharmacies, especially rural ones squeezed below cost by PBM reimbursement, would be paid at least the national average drug acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee, with post-claim clawback fees prohibited.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal program patients and community pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must reimburse in-network pharmacies for the national average drug acquisition cost of a drug plus a dispensing fee equal to what the state Medicaid program pays, ending reimbursement practices that often pay pharmacies less than the drug cost them [S2].

The bill prohibits spread pricing, steering to affiliated pharmacies, charging a beneficiary more than the pharmacy was reimbursed, forcing brand-name drugs when cheaper generics exist, and post-adjudication fees that cut pharmacy reimbursement [S2].

Beneficiaries' cost sharing at the point of sale must be calculated on a price reduced by at least 80% of all manufacturer rebates on the drug, so rebates lower what patients actually pay rather than flowing back to the PBM and plan [S2].

Knowingly and willfully violating the rules would be a felony carrying up to $1 million in fines per act or up to 10 years in prison, and private parties could bring False Claims Act-style civil suits against PBMs on behalf of the United States [S2].

The bill expands Medicaid drug price survey transparency to all pharmacy types (mail-order, specialty, long-term care, hospital) and requires public reporting of survey response rates and pharmacy price concessions, while barring use of non-retail pharmacy pricing to set retail reimbursement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The three dominant PBMs — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts (Cigna), and Optum Rx (UnitedHealth) — and their corporate parents would lose spread-pricing revenue, post-claim pharmacy fees, and the steering of patients toward their own affiliated pharmacies. Health plans and programs they administer could see higher pharmacy reimbursement costs, some of which could flow into premiums or federal spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: The big three PBMs and their parent insurers

drawbacks.text: A fixed reimbursement formula of national average acquisition cost plus a capped dispensing fee may not reflect what some pharmacies — especially specialty pharmacies buying through different channels — actually pay for expensive drugs, and could be set too low for high-cost therapies [S2].

Higher required pharmacy reimbursement means Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee plans, and TRICARE — and ultimately taxpayers and premium payers — could bear added drug benefit costs, since PBMs would no longer be able to offset pharmacy payments with spread revenue [S2].
The blanket prohibition on tying reimbursement to any performance scores or metrics could sweep in legitimate quality and adherence programs along with the manipulative ones [S2].

The combination of per-act felony penalties, $1 million fines, and private whistleblower suits would invite extensive litigation over what counts as a knowing violation, and smaller PBMs could face compliance costs that entrench the large incumbents the bill targets [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-side and pharmacy-side benefits are direct and concrete: cheaper point-of-sale costs from rebate pass-through, guaranteed access to in-network pharmacies, and a reimbursement floor for pharmacies operating at a loss. The main uncertainty is cost pass-through — eliminating spread pricing and clawbacks raises the underlying cost of the pharmacy benefit, and part of that could surface in premiums and federal outlays, though those costs today are largely hidden inside opaque PBM contracts. The enforcement design is aggressive and could be litigated heavily, but the core mechanics are straightforward rules that PBMs in Medicare and Medicaid already face under separate CMS rules adopted around the same period, suggesting they are administrable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four House committees, then to a Health subcommittee in December 2024, and no committee ever acted on it before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) introduced the Pharmacists Fight Back Act on July 23, 2024, joined as original cosponsor by Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-TN), herself a licensed pharmacist [S1][S2].

The bill was referred the same day to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Accountability, and Armed Services — a multi-committee referral that splits jurisdiction and makes advancement harder [S1][S4].
It drew 55 cosponsors, split between 29 of 224 House Republicans and 26 of 216 House Democrats [S3].
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the last action it received [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant pharmacy benefits managers and their parent companies are better off: the bill's bans on spread pricing, post-claim pharmacy fees, and steering to affiliated pharmacies never took effect, and the multi-committee referral plus subcommittee referral left the bill parked with no action until it expired.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefits managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill eliminates the core ways PBMs profit in federal drug programs: spread pricing, post-claim fees charged to pharmacies, steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies, and keeping rebates rather than passing them to patients at the counter. It also adds felony and whistleblower exposure for knowing violations. PBMs profit today by charging federal programs more than they pay pharmacies and by directing volume to their own retail operations, so their interest runs against both patients and independent pharmacies.

Pharmacies would be paid at least the national average drug acquisition cost plus a Medicaid-equivalent dispensing fee, and could no longer have claims reduced by post-adjudication fees. Independent pharmacies, which frequently fill prescriptions at a loss under PBM contracts, gain survival prospects; patients in rural areas where independent pharmacies are closing also gain from keeping them open.

The bill does not cap drug list prices or change manufacturer-PBM rebate negotiations, but it requires at least 80% of every rebate to reduce patient cost sharing, making high-rebate formulary positioning less valuable as a lever to keep pricier drugs on formularies over cheaper generics.

industries.industry: Medicare, Medicaid, FEHB, and TRICARE health plans and their insurers
industries.note: Plans must pass rebate value through to patients and pay pharmacies the full acquisition cost, which could raise their drug benefit costs; in return they gain transparent acquisition-cost data from the expanded Medicaid price surveys and a ban on PBM practices like spread pricing that opaque contracts previously concealed.
